extracted.intended_audience: TV industry followers, entertainment executives, producers, and Deadline readers
extracted.subtask_description: An honor-roll style industry roundup identifying producers, production companies and pods that landed multiple pilot orders during the 2017 broadcast pilot season, noting networks, studios, genres, and notable attachments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple pilot orders / juggling multiple pilots
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who 'beat the odds, and then some, juggling multiple pilots.' The piece highlights individuals and companies with several pilots in a single season.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples cited: Aaron Kaplan’s Kapital Entertainment with six pilots; Greg Berlanti’s Berlanti Productions with four pilots; 3 Arts Entertainment with five pilots. Use number of pilots in a season as an indicator of an entity's development momentum and success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pilots across multiple networks and studios
rubrics_metrics.description: Having pilot orders placed at several different networks and produced by multiple studios (e.g., 'six pilots — all comedy — at three networks with five different studios').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aaron Kaplan example shows value of spread: pilots at CBS, ABC and Fox and produced by multiple studios. Diversity across networks/studios signals broad marketability and relationships across the industry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pod / studio backing ('top pods' delivering commitments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Strong pods/studio groups translating development bets into pilot orders: 'Going into the development season, Warner Bros. TV and ABC Studios bet heavily on their top pods, and they delivered big commitments that translated into pilot orders.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by Berlanti Productions being behind a large share of WBTV’s pilots this season. Presence of influential pods/studios increases odds of pilot pickups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre breadth (comedy vs. drama; hourlong vs. half-hour; animation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Success measured by ability to land pilots across genres and formats — comedies, dramas, half-hour, hourlong, and animated presentations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Kapital’s all-comedy slate; Berlanti’s mix of three dramas and a comedy; Kapital also had an animated presentation. Having projects in multiple genres/formats demonstrates range and lowers dependency on a single market trend.

rubrics_metrics.name: Established creators/producers launching multiple pilots
rubrics_metrics.description: Well-known showrunners/creators securing multiple pilot orders in a season (e.g., Kenya Barris, Bill Lawrence, Shonda Rhimes, Greg Berlanti, Max Mutchnick).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article lists creators with several projects — often lending star power or track record that helps development. Track record and name recognition are implicit criteria for repeated greenlights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existing on-air series / track record of produced series
rubrics_metrics.description: Production companies/creators with several series currently on air are highlighted (e.g., Kapital has six series on the air; Berlanti has six series; Marvel Television has multiple series).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Having active series is framed as part of why companies can land multiple pilots — it evidences production capacity, network relationships, and past success.

rubrics_metrics.name: High-profile talent attachments (stars, showrunners, directors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Attachment of recognizable actors, writers or directors to pilots (e.g., Felicity Huffman, Toni Collette, Lucy Hale, Dean Georgaris, Simon Kinberg) as a factor in pilot orders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece repeatedly mentions notable names attached to projects; such attachments are presented as increasing a pilot’s profile and likelihood of being ordered.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-season / new-company success
rubrics_metrics.description: Newly launched companies or companies in their first full development season landing multiple pilot orders (e.g., Keshet Studios in its first full season, Secret Hideout in its first development season).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article uses these examples to show that new entrants can immediately make impact; landing multiple pilots in a debut season is presented as a noteworthy achievement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Straight-to-series and cross-platform strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-traditional ordering routes and platform tie-ins (e.g., straight-to-series orders, Imax theatrical debuts for first episodes, shows on streaming platforms like CBS All Access and Netflix).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Marvel’s The Inhumans was straight-to-series with first two episodes debuting in Imax; Secret Hideout’s Star Trek is on CBS All Access. These strategies reflect alternate success pathways beyond traditional broadcast pilot pickups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leveraging existing IP: spinoffs, revivals, and companions
rubrics_metrics.description: Networks ordering spinoffs, revivals or companion series to existing successful shows (e.g., Black-ish spinoff, Will & Grace companion, Will & Grace revival).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article shows networks use established IP as a lower-risk development strategy; spinoffs/companions/revivals are presented as a common route to pilot orders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Director pedigree / veteran helmer involvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Experienced directors securing multiple pilot directing gigs in a season (e.g., James Burrows and Pam Fryman lining up multiple directing jobs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Veteran multi-camera directors are highlighted as reliable choices for pilots, implying director reputation can influence pilot production and potential success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feature film talent transitioning to TV (feature scribe / producer moves)
rubrics_metrics.description: Feature writers/producers making successful transitions to television with pilot orders (e.g., Dean Georgaris, Simon Kinberg).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Feature-to-TV transitions are noted as another route to pilot orders; the presence of film talent is used to underline production value or prestige.
